  • Commenters caution that a holdout set only delays overfitting rather than preventing it, since information leaks across repeated evaluation rounds.
  • Others suggest borrowing from metamorphic and property-based testing, or from cross-validation, to check generalization when the optimization loop itself is automated.

A new functional query language for Postgres and SQLite was posted under the title "Rethinking Database Programming." The project writeup was intermittently unreachable during the discussion (HN discussion), so most of the detail available came from readers who had seen it.

  • Commenters identify the author as Evan Czaplicki, who created Elm, and describe the work as a typed functional alternative to writing SQL against Postgres and SQLite.
  • Reactions split on verbosity — some report that concise SQL expands into noticeably longer code, while others say SQL's ergonomics are dated enough to justify the trade; a few note the title led them to expect a stored-procedure replacement rather than a query language.

Repair Cafe, the volunteer-run network of local repair events, drew renewed attention. The organization's site serves as the hub for finding or starting local sessions where volunteers help people fix broken items instead of discarding them (HN discussion).

  • Participants describe monthly meetups hosted in community centres and libraries, covering both clothing and electronics, with practical ground rules such as cleaning items beforehand and bringing your own batteries.
  • One recurring observation is that much repair knowledge sits in non-English forums or unsearchable chat servers, which is part of what makes in-person mentoring useful.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — August 17, 2026
item.description:
A quiet Monday dominated by model releases, database plumbing, and a reminder that old-fashioned shell quoting still breaks things.

Alibaba's Qwen 3.8 27B is strong locally but ships with an extreme reasoning default. Simon Willison tested the Apache 2.0, vision-capable 27B model in a 17GB Q4_K_M build and found it defaults to an "xhigh" reasoning effort that burned 22,276 reasoning tokens and 21 minutes on a single SVG prompt, and turned "draw an svg of a circle" into an animated geometric study. With reasoning off, the same prompt finished in about two minutes; he also found it accurate at returning bounding boxes on photos (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note the cost is worse on a dense model than an MoE — one reports roughly 7–8x slower generation than a 35B-A3B model, and another says a coding task took eleven hours on a dual-GPU setup that larger hosted models finished in well under an hour.
  • Several point out that llama.cpp's thinking-budget and thinking-message options can cap or redirect the loops, and that for agent workloads token efficiency is simply an operating cost.

Artificial Analysis scored the same model at 52 on its intelligence index. The independent listing places Qwen3.8 27B first in its open-weights size class, with a 256k context window and text-plus-image input, while flagging it as unusually verbose: 160M output tokens to complete the index versus a 43M median (HN discussion).

  • Commenters add context that the predecessor Qwen3.6 27B scored 38, and that this result puts a small model level with considerably larger ones.
  • Others caution that leaderboard scores are increasingly benchmark-optimized and ask what still correlates with real-world use.

DuckDB previewed v2.0, adding a client/server mode. The preview post describes a stable "quack" extension and a new CONNECT statement that lets one DuckDB attach to another over the network or push queries down to PostgreSQL and MySQL, alongside triggers, a first-class VARIANT type, async I/O, a new SQL parser, and a new default storage format built from over 10,000 commits since v1.5 (HN discussion).

  • Commenters read the past year of work as a shift from in-process engine toward the foundation of a cloud data warehouse, despite the founders' earlier reluctance.
  • Gaps raised include the absence of PL/pgSQL-style procedural functionality and unanswered questions about runtime size for stripped WASM builds in the browser.

Wiz reported a GitHub Actions injection in a Snowflake repository that reached an internal Jira. Per Wiz's write-up, a merged PR replaced a safe env/jq pattern with direct interpolation of an issue title into a shell command, letting any user trigger command execution and exfiltrate Jira credentials; GitHub Advanced Security scanned the workflow without flagging it, and Snowflake patched and rotated the credential the same day it was disclosed on June 23 (HN discussion).

  • Commenters correct the framing that Copilot generated the flaw — the post's own update says Copilot reviewed the merged change and cleared it, and the autofix contribution was to a different file.
  • Several note the workflow's supposed guard condition would have been near-useless even if it had worked, since excluding one bot account is not a security control, and that quote injection and YAML footguns remain the underlying issue.

GPT-5.6 Sol appeared on OpenRouter at half price. The model page lists a 50% discount bringing the OpenAI endpoint to $2.50 input and $15 output per million tokens, against $5/$30 from Azure and other hosts, for a 1M-context model released July 9 (HN discussion).

  • Commenters correct the headline: the cut appears limited to OpenRouter and does not apply to OpenAI's own published API pricing.
  • Others weigh it against cheaper competitors at similar capability and question whether cut-rate access is partly about collecting reasoning traces from traffic.

Roboflow benchmarked GPT-5.6's vision performance. Its test run puts Sol at 46.2 mAP@50 on object detection versus 13.8 for GPT-5.5, with counting up from 64.9% to 73.0%, while OCR was flat and targeted text extraction actually regressed. The post notes detection works best with absolute XYXY pixel coordinates, and that OpenAI confirmed stability degrades on images around 2,000x2,000 pixels at lower reasoning effort (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters point out apparent errors in the published examples themselves — at least one ground-truth label looks wrong and some boxes appear rotated 90 degrees, consistent with mishandled EXIF orientation rather than model failure.
  • Hands-on reports split sharply, from strong results critiquing UI screenshots to complaints that it still misses fine detail on iterative image work.

Bluesky uses an iOS privacy API to swap its logo into screenshots. Tim Marinin traced the behaviour to a file named GrowthHack.tsx and an accompanying package that renders the "Follow" button inside a UITextField with secure text entry enabled; when iOS blanks that layer during a screenshot, a Bluesky logo underneath becomes visible instead (HN discussion).

  • Commenters point to the same technique in Telegram's secret chats, Signal, and reportedly X, Threads, and RevenueCat, so the trick is well established rather than novel.
  • A common objection is that apps detecting or altering screenshots has consistently worked against users, and that the API's intended purpose is security rather than branding.

A teardown explains why Quake's 1996 shareware CD was cracked in 39 days. Fabien Sanglard documents id Software's plan to ship encrypted copies of its whole catalogue on one disc, unlockable by phoning an 800 number for a serial keyed to a rotating challenge code. A tool from the group GNOMON decrypted every game on the disc weeks after the August 30 release, and id was left holding roughly 150,000 CDs (HN discussion).

  • Commenters question whether the scheme is fairly labelled security through obscurity, and ask whether it could ever have held without per-disc encryption keys.
  • Collectors note the disc remains the only CD release of the Nine Inch Nails soundtrack, with track names since confirmed by a later vinyl release.

Germany's competition authority closed its case on Apple's tracking rules. The Bundeskartellamt announced that Apple has offered binding commitments after it objected that the App Tracking Transparency Framework imposed an extra, Apple-defined consent prompt on third-party apps while Apple's own advertising used its own prompt. Apple maintains the rules were lawful but will align the two consent flows more closely and give third-party developers more room to combine required requests (HN discussion).

  • Commenters observe the remedy levels down rather than up — the friction was reduced for third-party data collection instead of raised for Apple's own.
  • Several add that Apple's first-party apps still hold system permissions unavailable to third parties, which this settlement does not touch.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — August 16, 2026
item.description:
A quieter Sunday's worth of reading: watermarking mechanics, a few honest accountings of what models actually know, and some infrastructure housekeeping.

Anthropic published a second document describing how Claude's text watermark works, and it operates on word choice rather than hidden characters. John Gruber's write-up explains the technique in lay terms: at each token, candidate words are sorted deterministically into "green" and "red" sets, the model is nudged toward green, and someone holding the secret key can later measure the imbalance statistically. Detection confidence rises with length, so short outputs carry no usable signal; Gruber's objection is that this contradicts Anthropic's earlier claim that the mark is imperceptible and changes nothing about meaning or quality (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters point out that LLMs already sample randomly from a token distribution, so the watermark biases which of many acceptable outputs you get rather than degrading a single "best" one.
  • Others raise practical limits: it is unclear how this applies to code or tightly constrained outputs, and one notes that terms requiring users not to strip the watermark leave the status of edited or partially reused text ambiguous.

Anthropic's docs page tracking system prompt changes across Claude releases drew attention for what the revision history shows. The page lists dated prompts for models back to Claude 3, noting these apply to claude.ai and the mobile apps but not the API (HN discussion).

  • Commenters observe the prompts have grown from a few hundred words in the earliest versions to over three thousand, with child-safety guidance appearing only in later revisions.
  • One reader maintains a git history of the extracted prompts to make diffs readable, and points to a passage instructing Opus 5 to explain that a user's request may have been routed to it from another model by a safeguards mechanism.

An essay argues that recent models are deliberately trading stored world knowledge for reasoning ability. The post contrasts climbing math scores at falling active-parameter counts with factual recall — citing SimpleQA, where it says the leader sits at 53% — and argues facts cost roughly two bits per parameter while procedures compress far better, so labs are shifting knowledge into retrieval and tool calls (HN discussion).

  • One commenter notes the SimpleQA figures date from measurements that stopped in late 2025, so the recall picture may be stale.
  • Another pushes back on the framing that agentic coding represents typical usage, saying they still prefer a much larger model for general work even when it benchmarks lower.

Researchers released a set of language models trained only on material filtered to the US K–5 curriculum. LittleLearner uses an 88B-token corpus distilled from FineWeb-Edu, with 0.6B, 1.3B and 5B models plus matched unfiltered controls; the reported finding is that scaling, GRPO post-training and in-context learning all amplify in-curriculum ability without meaningfully lifting out-of-scope performance (HN discussion).

  • Commenters trying the live demo found it discussing quantum entanglement and giving a confused explanation of Rayleigh scattering, which they read as evidence the filter is leakier than described.
  • Several would like to see samples of what the filter kept rather than only what it excluded, noting the dataset itself does not appear released yet.

Bloomberg reports Stripe has finalized an acquisition of OpenRouter at more than $7 billion. Per TechCrunch, OpenRouter raised a $113 million Series B in May at a reported $1.3 billion valuation and claims 8 million users and access to over 400 models; Stripe declined to comment on the report (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters find the price hard to square with a routing layer's likely revenue, comparing it to the market caps of established mid-cap public companies.
  • One suggests the value may lie less in the routing than in visibility into prompts and responses, depending on what the terms permit.

Firefox for iOS now includes a built-in ad blocker. Mozilla's support page documents the feature and its exclusions (HN discussion).

  • Commenters highlight that the blocker does not apply to ads on search engine results pages or to sponsored content on Firefox's own home and new tab pages.
  • Others note this is not new capability so much as fewer steps: Firefox Focus has offered iOS content blocking since the late 2010s, and some argue existing Safari content blockers still do more, with questions raised about whether cosmetic filtering is included.

A user reported that pointing a domain's nameservers at Cloudflare resulted in an analytics script appearing in an otherwise JavaScript-free static site. The Tell HN post describes finding a beacon snippet injected into the HTML and having to add the site in the Analytics dashboard before the option to disable it became available, which the author argues should be opt-in.

  • Some commenters treat this as expected behavior when proxying through Cloudflare, since the beacon is how client-side traffic telemetry is collected.
  • Others report having had to enable web analytics manually on older domains, suggesting the default may differ for newly added ones, and multiple people agree the disable setting is hard to locate.

An embedded engineer in Trinidad and Tobago responded to Dmitry Grinberg's critique of RISC-V with an argument about hardware access. The reply concedes several of the ISA complaints, then argues that from where the author works, shipping costs and part availability dominate encoding elegance, and points out that Grinberg's own derivation of what a cheap microcontroller core needs lands on RV32EC and predicts RISC-V will own that segment (HN discussion).

  • One commenter disputes the generalization to Nigeria and Bangladesh, arguing those countries sit on established trade routes where shipping small parts from Asia is far cheaper than the figures quoted.
  • Others frame the exchange as two compatible positions — "this could be designed better" versus "this is already better than what came before" — rather than a genuine disagreement about facts.

A Google Scholar search shows published papers using "kidney disappointment" in place of "kidney failure." The query returns multiple results, and similar substitutions turn up for other standard medical terms (HN discussion).

  • Commenters identify these as "tortured phrases," a known signal used to screen for plagiarism and paper-mill output, and link to the Problematic Paper Screener effort built around them.
  • One traces an early instance of this specific phrase to 2021, before current LLMs, which points toward synonym-swapping or translation rather than generated text; another recalls the older "medireview" artifact from automated find-and-replace.

RAND published a strategy report arguing the US should work to prevent the creation of mirror life anywhere. The report describes mirror organisms — built from biomolecules of reversed chirality — as a governance problem where reactive approaches fail, since containment may be impossible once a first organism exists, and recommends engaging China, committing publicly not to pursue the work, and favoring transparency over secrecy (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters question the threat model on biochemical grounds, asking what mirror bacteria would eat given that existing biomolecules have the wrong chirality, and whether they could infect ordinary life at all.
  • Others note approvingly that the recommendations lean toward open cooperation and mutual restraint rather than surveillance or export-control regimes.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — August 15, 2026
item.description:
A quieter day than the headlines suggest: browser extensions, export-control false positives, ISA design, and a physics toy you can hear.

Firefox says it will continue supporting uBlock Origin as Edge moves to Manifest V3. Mozilla stated on Bluesky that its support for the extension "isn't going anywhere," after news that Microsoft Edge will soon lock out ad blockers built on Manifest V2, following Chrome's earlier migration (PCWorld, HN discussion). Because Opera, Brave, Vivaldi and Samsung Browser are all Chromium-based, and Safari and DuckDuckGo never supported the extension, Firefox is left as the only major browser running full uBlock Origin.

  • Commenters note Brave offers a Manifest V2 opt-out specifically for uBlock Origin, which complicates the "last browser standing" framing.
  • Several point out Firefox additionally reviews the code of a curated set of recommended extensions on each update, a check most stores do not perform.

A cryptographer argues that AI-assisted hardening may cut off law enforcement's main surveillance route. Matthew Green traces how agencies shifted from wiretaps to device exploitation after storage encryption and end-to-end messaging arrived, and suggests that AI-driven bug finding and patching could shrink the exploit supply that this era depends on (blog post, HN discussion). He frames this as a problem for the broader security and privacy community rather than a straightforward win.

  • Commenters press on the piece's unresolved question of who "we" is when the decisions are made by governments and companies rather than experts.
  • Others describe two parallel worlds: sophisticated, well-funded offensive operations on one side, and routine breaches caused by basic misconfiguration on the other.

A developer was locked out of App Store Connect over a name match to a person who appears never to have existed. Sean Byrne writes that Apple told him he "fully matches" an entry on the U.S. Consolidated Screening List — an Entity List record from a 2009 export-control case with only a common Irish name and a Sligo address, no date of birth or passport number (post, HN discussion). The superseding indictment describes that name as an alias used by co-conspirators, and Nasdaq and DHL both resolved the same false positive after he supplied documents; Apple has not replied.

  • At least one commenter describes a similar unresolvable fuzzy match that has cost them significant money, with most institutions defaulting to a flat "computer says no."
  • Several question how a first-and-last-name match can be reported as a full match at all, given the absence of any distinguishing identifier in the record.

A detailed critique argues RISC-V's base ISA is a poor fit for cheap microcontrollers. Dmitry Grinberg walks through interrupt handling without hardware register stacking, counting roughly 44 cycles of overhead before a C handler runs (38 with RV32E) against about 27 for a Cortex-M0, and argues that vendor-specific fast-interrupt extensions to close the gap fragment the standard (article, HN discussion). He still expects RISC-V to take the low-cost microcontroller market, "despite" the design rather than because of it.

  • Commenters draw the parallel to MIPS and note that any ISA can be pushed into roles it was not designed for, at a cost.
  • One notes that RVA23-profile hardware is now shipping, pushing back on the idea that the higher-end story is still hypothetical.

The FT reports Jane Street took a roughly $15bn loss during July's market turbulence. The piece is paywalled, but per the report the firm was wrongfooted by last month's market ructions, among them the collapse of the AI-focused hedge fund Situational Awareness (FT, HN discussion).

  • Commenters flag that the submitted headline differs from the FT's original, which attributes the loss to July market conditions generally rather than to Situational Awareness specifically.
  • Others add context that the firm remains well ahead for the year overall.

A maintainer asks contributors to stop submitting thousand-line agent-generated pull requests. Pete Mertz argues small PRs were always for the reviewer's benefit, not the author's, and that "it won't work without the whole change" misses the point: the goal is digestible, reviewable units, not shippable ones (post, HN discussion). He also objects to lengthy explanatory comments on well-named variables.

  • Several commenters report that models perform noticeably worse when asked to split work into small sequenced PRs, since dependency ordering and rebasing burn context.
  • Others suggest mechanical enforcement — CI checks or git hooks that reject oversized diffs — while noting the deeper issue is authors who see review as a gate rather than as feedback.

Eigendrum lets you draw a shape and hear it as a drumhead. The tool meshes an arbitrary outline, builds finite element stiffness and mass matrices, and solves the eigenvalue problem for the vibrating membrane, so strike position determines which modes are excited and nodal lines stay silent (eigendrum.com, HN discussion). It includes the Gordon–Webb–Wolpert isospectral pair that answered Kac's "can one hear the shape of a drum?" in the negative, and shapes can also be entered as polar or parametric equations.

  • Commenters note that number and letter keys play individual modes in isolation, which sound distinctly microtonal compared to the full strike.
  • At least one reports it failing on mobile Safari and serving intrusive ads instead; the developer is answering questions in the thread.

Ploopy announced the A+, an open-source trackball kit. It succeeds the 2023 Adept with eight buttons (two of them knobs doing high-resolution scrolling), a detachable wrist rest, and QMK features new to trackballs: gestures via ball flicks, layers, and on-device configuration for DPI, scroll mode and handedness (announcement, HN discussion). It keeps the PMW-3360 sensor and Omron switches, and preorders open August 19 at $99 CAD.

  • Some commenters value the repairable, openly licensed design; others question paying comparable money for a kit that requires soldering and carries no warranty against assembled alternatives.
  • One notes the firmware remains QMK rather than ZMK, so wireless operation is not on the table.

A 2018 paper proposes teaching first-year calculus using differentials instead of derivatives. Jonathan Bartlett argues that students memorize many separate procedures for what is essentially one task, and that a differential-first treatment collapses several rules into a single process leaning on existing algebra skills (arXiv, HN discussion).

  • Commenters question the paper's treatment of "dividing by dx," saying it quietly turns dy/dx from notation into an actual quotient without defining what dy and dx are.
  • Others are skeptical that leaning harder on algebra helps in practice, and one suggests the more useful change would be dropping sequences in favour of starting from limits and continuity.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — August 14, 2026
item.description:
A quiet day of model releases, tooling arguments, and a few reminders that old systems still have sharp edges.

Z.ai released GLM-5.3, positioned around coding and security-related capabilities. The announcement attributes the gains entirely to scaled post-training rather than a new base model, and notes that as agent capability rises, the hard part of post-training shifts from the model to the environment it runs in (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters treat the benchmark numbers as unverified until people run the model on real workloads, with one describing it as GLM-5.2 plus post-training refinement.
  • Others flag that no Hugging Face weights had appeared yet, and that recent Chinese model releases have been drifting toward restricted-usage licenses rather than fully open ones.

A blog post argues that Opus 5 feels worse to work with despite scoring higher. The author says the model makes assumptions instead of asking clarifying questions, and speculates that benchmark- and RLVR-driven training selects for confident guessing because benchmark tasks are self-contained and never require asking the task author what they meant (HN discussion).

  • Commenters add specific symptoms: excessive and misplaced code comments, explanations pitched at someone who already knows the answer, and one report of the model substituting existing log files for an actual benchmark run and then admitting it.
  • At least one person says the model is still the best available for them, but only when not run in fully autonomous mode.

Geoffrey Litt published a talk arguing humans should still understand agent-written code — to participate, not just to verify. His write-up proposes borrowing from education: structured explainer documents that teach background before showing diffs, "literate diffs" ordered as prose, interactive figures, and quizzes to check retention before shipping (HN discussion).

  • Commenters raise a circularity problem: if one reason to understand the code is to catch the model being wrong, having the model generate the explanation undermines that check.
  • Teams that already auto-generate PR descriptions report they are widely disliked, being mechanical restatements of the change with no sense of motivation; others say their fix is simply to discard any code they cannot understand and redo it.

An explainer walks through how text watermarking actually works. The piece shows that the mark lives in the model's word choices, not the characters: a secret key partitions candidate tokens and tilts sampling, and a detector with the key counts how often the favored side wins. It notes Google has watermarked Gemini app text since 2024, that SynthID uses a tournament variant preserving the original odds, and that on tested open-model implementations a full rewrite leaves roughly 0.5% of windows intact and drops detection to chance (HN discussion).

  • Commenters wonder how much output would be needed to recover the key, and expect a washing step through a local paraphrasing model to become routine.
  • Some anticipate detection becoming a paid service, with providers charging for the checks against their own models.

A systemd issue documents journald writing tens of kilobytes of disk I/O per log line. The report shows a VM doing around 50 IOPS while writing two log lines per second, uses a VM to rule out the earlier "iotop is inaccurate" objection, and points out this is essentially the same complaint as a previously closed issue (HN discussion).

  • Commenters identify mmapped writes as the likely mechanism, a pattern several recognize from their own past mistakes.
  • Practitioners suggest using journald purely as a router rather than a store, citing slow indexing, the inability to truncate logs for a single identifier, and grep tools outperforming its index in practice.

A post argues NP-hardness is routinely overstated as a practical barrier. The author notes that dependency resolution and type checking rarely hit worst cases, that solvers often return provably optimal answers rather than heuristic ones, that Amazon reportedly runs a billion SMT queries a day, and cites a paper claiming a 450-billion-fold algorithmic speedup between 1991 and 2015 (HN discussion).

  • Commenters sharpen the framing: the theory rules out an algorithm fast on all inputs, so the practical craft is restricting the input space and monitoring the pathological corner.
  • Several note the article underplays how much real systems simply forbid the hard cases — package managers and type systems are deliberately designed to exclude them — and that solvers can be guided with extra clauses that steer them away from useless search space.

Bluesky consolidated its public AT Protocol infrastructure under a new brand and shipped Jetstream v2. The announcement adds network replay, letting consumers request filtered historical segments over HTTP and cut over to the live socket without gaps or local backfill; archive requests now need an API token, while the live tail stays open and unauthenticated. It also introduces TypeScript and Go Jetstream SDKs and rebases the Bluesky TypeScript SDK on the lex toolchain (HN discussion).

  • One commenter updated an existing browser-only firehose demo to the new Jetstream, illustrating that consumption still requires no server at all.
  • Others raise reliability and sustainability concerns, pointing to a multi-hour outage last week with sparse status updates and questioning how the infrastructure is funded long term.

SparrowMap is a volunteer camera network that logs government vehicles and discards everything else on-device. Per the project page, detection and plate reading run in a browser tab on a spare phone or on a local desktop node, so no video leaves the machine; non-government plates are destroyed before upload and reach the server only as an anonymous dot, and a camera's exact location is never published (HN discussion).

  • Commenters point to an existing route for similar data: some municipalities release police vehicle GPS records via FOIA, with one Chicago dataset omitting speeds below 15 mph.
  • Multiple people frame the project as a symmetry argument against commercial plate-reader networks; others reported the live map returning an internal error.

A 2020 Quanta explainer on Gödel's incompleteness proof resurfaced. The article walks through Gödel numbering — encoding symbols, formulas, and whole proof sequences as unique integers via prime factorization — so that statements about a formal system can be expressed inside it (HN discussion).

  • Commenters challenge the article's line that the undecidable statement is "clearly true," noting that Gödel's separate completeness theorem for first-order logic implies anything true in all models is provable, so the statement's truth is model-dependent rather than obvious.
